I'm not going to recommend any specific models, since this usually just turns in to a pissing match. However, I'd offer these tips:

1) Don't buy AMD mobile anything. Just don't. Not processors, not graphics. Do not buy intel integrated video unless it's a secondary graphics adapter - some laptops will dynamically switch between two chips for 2d and 3d performance/less power consumption. Intel CPU with nVidia graphics hardware remains the best overall combination. It is generally more expensive, but has greater performance and generally has fewer problems.

2) You want an nvidia 760m or better. With nvidia model numbers, the second number is the important one. Model numbers follow the GMS format. The first number is generation, the second number is model. the third number is sub-model. So a 970m is generation 9, model 7, submodel 0, the "m" denotes "mobile". The current generation is 10. Higher model number is generally better performance, higher generation is usually a smaller die and better (less) power consumption than previous generations. More power usage means more heat. Generation 7 or better, and model 6 or better is preferred. Avoid model 4 or 5 regardless of generation.

3) The 1000m series is out, and is far more powerful than the 900 series, but will cost proportionately more. You may be better off looking at previous generations if possible.

4) Unless it comes with one, be prepared to buy an SSD to replace the drive inside the laptop. It generally costs $100 - $200 It's totally worth it as it will give you a significant performance improvement.

5) No less than 6gb of system ram, 8gb is optimal. More is better, but more than 12gb is overkill.

6) Any intel i5 or i7 made in the last 5 - 7 years. Buying older intel generations can save you A LOT of money. This includes Haswell, Broadwell, Skylake, or Icelake architecture and their subcategories running at 2.66ghz or greater. Clock speed is not as much of a concern as it used to be. Many games that say they optimally need 3ghz+ often run just fine with less. If buying an i7, triple channel ram or the option to add it is preferable. Keep in mind than you do not need an i7 for a good gaming experience, a less expensive i5 will work great. Avoid i3 (underpowered) and Xenon processors.

7) Always note potential upgrade paths. Most laptops have removable memory and hard drives, some have removable GPU/CPU chips. Some laptops may solder components to the board - you want to know this ahead of time.

8) Remember the operating system. Almost all retail-purchased laptops will come with an OS, but if you buy used (which is something to consider) you may need to set aside money to buy an OS. If you have strong reservations against Windows 10 you may need to set aside even more money for a Windows 7 license as this is usually more expensive due to scarcity.

9) If at ANY point you want to use Linux/SteamOS, find out the chipset of the wireless and wired network adapters, as well as the audio chipset and ensure it's compatible. If you don't have any interest in Linux or SteamOS, skip this. Never just assume a laptop won't have problems with Linux. Personally I think gaming on Linux is a waste of time but this is about you, not me.

10) READ REVIEWS. I don't care how much someone likes X, Y, or Z - it is ALWAYS your responsibility to verify any information you get before making a purchase. Always read 2 or 3 reviews dealing with the same laptop and/or hardware from different people. Sometimes laptops have design defects, you want to know these things before a purchase. Never impulse buy a laptop.
